newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Army ex-paratrooper found guilty of N.C. murders.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Army ex-paratrooper found guilty of N.C. murders.

text.p: A jury on Friday found a former Fort Bragg paratrooper, Malcolm Wright, guilty of two counts of first-degree murder in the racially motivated shooting of a black couple that prompted the Army to undertake a national investigation of racism in its ranks.

Wright also was found guilty on one count of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder for the deaths of Jackie Burden and Michael James, who were gunned down as they walked down a street in Fayetteville, North Carolina, on Dec. 7, 1995.

The jury of 11 whites and one black deliberated for about 45 minutes on Thursday afternoon before resuming on Friday morning. They deliberated for about six hours on Friday before returning the unanimous guilty verdicts.

A hearing to determine whether Wright, 22, of Lexington, Kentucky, who is white, will be executed or spend his life in prison was scheduled to begin before the same jury and judge, North Carolina Senior Superior Court Judge Coy Brewer, on Monday morning.

Wright stared straight ahead as each juror was polled, never turning to face the panel, one member of which, a woman, appeared to be crying. His father, Malcolm Wright Sr., looked disgusted and his mother cried.
Wright's family did not speak to reporters.

Karon Knox, Michael James's sister, expressed relief. "We're pleased with the verdict. It's been a long year for us since this happened. We're particularly thankful to the entire judicial system and I personally have faith in our judicial system again."
One of Wright's court-appointed attorneys, Paul Herzog, immediately asked Judge Brewer to set aside the verdict, a motion that was denied.
He also asked that the death penalty not be considered in sentencing, which also was denied.

James Burmeister, 21, of Thompson, Pennsylvania, like Wright a member of a skinhead group at Fort Bragg, was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to life in prison earlier this year in connection with the killings.

He was found guilty of shooting James, 36, and Burden, 27, at point-blank range, killings that led Army Secretary Togo West to initiate a national investigation into racist activity into military ranks. The probe found little evidence of overt racism, but 22 people were subsequently discharged, including Burmeister, Wright and Randy Meadows, a third soldier charged in the crime who testified against the other two.
Burmeister, Wright and Meadows were all members of Fort Bragg's elite 82nd Airborne Division.
In finding Wright guilty of first-degree rather than second-degree murder, the jury apparently accepted the prosecutors' argument that Wright was culpable even though he did not fire the fatal shots.

"To me, he's just as guilty as if he pulled the trigger because he could have stopped it," said Julia Burden, Jackie Burden's aunt, after the verdict. "I think in his heart, he thinks he did right. He has never shown any remorse."

Wright's trial had been moved to New Hanover County Superior Court in Wilmington because of pretrial publicity stemming from Burmeister's conviction. Burmeister's jury had deadlocked 11-1 in favour of executing him.
Meadows, who has pleaded guilty to assault charges in connection with the slayings, was due to be sentenced after the Wright sentencing.
